Here is the itemized extraction from J. B. Lightfoot’s Saint Paul's Epistle to the Galatians: A Revised Text with Introduction, Notes, and Dissertations (1914 edition / 1890 10th edition text) covering the requested analytical criteria across all twelve B001 items.
1. B001-1: Romans 4:3 / Genesis 15:6 (Galatians 3:6)
Page / Locator: Page 136 (Note on Gal 3:6) & Pages 158–164 (Detached Note: "The Faith of Abraham").
Discusses a Competing Textual Form:
On page 136, Lightfoot notes that the Hebrew MT of Genesis 15:6 reads וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ לּוֹ צְדָקָה ("and [He] imputed it to him [for] righteousness"), whereas the Septuagint converts the active Hebrew verb into a passive construction (καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην). He observes that Paul quotes the LXX text verbatim in Galatians 3:6 and Romans 4:3, as do James 2:23, 1 Clement 10, and Justin Martyr (Dial. 119) [p. 136]
1
.
On page 136, Lightfoot notes that the Epistle of Barnabas (§ 13) quotes the passage "too loosely and with too obvious an infusion of St Paul's language to allow of any inference as to the text used by the writer" [p. 136]
1
.
On page 162 (fn. 1), Lightfoot documents that later Jewish Rabbinic writers altered the interpretation of Genesis 15:6 to read "And Abraham counted on God's righteousness" (making Abraham the subject of both clauses) specifically to cut the ground from under Paul's inference of righteousness by faith [p. 162]
2
.
On page 156 (fn. 4) & page 162, Lightfoot notes Aramaic dialectal forms (Targum of Jonathan rendering faith as הימנותא in Gen 15:6) and Syriac renderings (הימנותא) [p. 156, 162]
2
3
.
Disagrees with Another Scholar:
On page 164 (fn. 1), Lightfoot explicitly disagrees with commentators who view James 2:24 as a direct attack on Paul or Pauline converts; he agrees with Michaelis and Neander that James targets a Pharisaic barren orthodoxy [p. 164]
4
.
On page 157 (fn. 1), Lightfoot disagrees with Prof. Benjamin Jowett's general theory regarding the looseness of Paul's language ("an entire mistake"), while acknowledging Jowett's protest against over-subtle restrictions of meaning [p. 157]
5
.

On page 120, Lightfoot provides a cross-reference to 1 Corinthians 1:19 and Luke 7:30 to fix the exact sense of ἀθετῶ ("to nullify / set at nought"), comparing LXX Psalm 34:7 (where Symmachus substituted ἀναιτίως for Hebrew חִנָּם) [p. 120]

12. B001-12: Galatians 3:13 / Deuteronomy 21:23
Page / Locator: Pages 139–140 (Note on Gal 3:13) & Pages 152–154 (Detached Note: "The Interpretation of Deut. xxi. 23").
Notes a Hebrew / Greek Ambiguity:
On page 152, Lightfoot analyzes the grammatical ambiguity of קִלְלַת אֱלֹהִים in Deuteronomy 21:23: אֱלֹהִים can function as either a subjective genitive ("accursed of God", as in Judges 9:57) or an objective genitive ("an insult / reproach / contempt to God", as in Gen 27:13) [p. 152]
7
.
Discusses Competing Textual Forms:
On pages 152–153, Lightfoot evaluates multiple competing versions:
Septuagint: κεκατηραμένος ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ ("accursed in the sight of God");
Jewish/Ebionite Greek translators: Aquila and Theodotion (κατάρα Θεοῦ κρεμάμενος), Symmachus ("quia propter blasphemiam Dei suspensus est");
Apocryphal / Patristic Jewish-Christian citations: Ebionite Gospel ("ὕβρις Θεοῦ ὁ κρεμάμενος"), Ariston of Pella in the Dispute of Jason and Papiscus (λοιδορία Θεοῦ ὁ κρεμάμενος);
Rabbinic & Aramaic Targums: Siphri ("a reviling of God"), Targum of Pseudo-Jonathan, and Peshito Syriac [pp. 152–153]
7
unfold_less
8
9
.
Allows Authorial Adaptation & Intentional Omission:
On page 140, Lightfoot points out that Paul instinctively omits ὑπὸ Θεοῦ from LXX Deuteronomy 21:23 in Galatians 3:13 (ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς ὁ κρεμάμενος ἐπὶ ξύλου): "He was in no literal sense κατάρατος ὑπὸ Θεοῦ, and St Paul instinctively omits those words which do not strictly apply, and which, if added, would have required some qualification" [p. 140]
10
.
On page 154, Lightfoot explains Paul's adaptation in applying a statute originally concerning the post-execution exposure/gibbeting of a corpse to death by crucifixion, noting that Jewish national sentiment attached the ignominy to the hanging itself [p. 154].
Disagrees with Another Scholar:
On page 152, Lightfoot rejects interpretations that abandon the LXX subjective genitive, demonstrating that the LXX rendering suits the context best and is supported by direct biblical parallels (Judges 9:57) [p. 152]
7
.

164 EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS.  tain sense indeed the Messiah may be said to have been the object of Abraham’s faith ; for He, as the fulfilment of the promise, must have been dimly discerned by Abraham, as by one ‘looking through a glass darkly,’ And to this vague presentiment of a future Triumph or Redemption we may perhaps refer our Lord’s words (John viii. 56), ‘Your father Abraham rejoiced to see My day: and he saw it and was glad’ But however this may be, St Paul makes no such application of Abraham’s example. He does not once allude to the Christ, as the object of the patriarch’s faith.  To return once again to the passages from Jewish writers already cited : they are important in their bearing on the interpretation of the Apostolic writings in yet another point of view. The example of Abraham is quoted both by St Paul and St James ; while the deductions which the two Apostles draw from it are at first sight diametrically opposed in terms. ‘We con- clude that a man is justified by faith apart from (ywpis) works of law, says St Paul (Rom. iii. 28). ‘A man is justified of works and not of faith only, are the words of St James (ii. 24). Now, so long as our range of view is  confined to the Apostolic writings, it seems scarcely possible to resist the impression that St James is attacking the teaching, if not of St Paul him- self, at least of those who exaggerated and perverted it. But when we realise the fact that the passage in Genesis was a common thesis in the  Compari- son of St Paul and St James,  illustrated schools of the day, that the meaning of jaith was variously explained by  by the the disputants, that diverse lessons were drawn from it—then the case is  ae as altered. The Gentile Apostle and the Pharisaic Rabbi might both maintain the supremacy of faith as the means of salvation: but faith with St Paul was a very different thing from faith with Maimonides for instance. With the one its prominent idea is a spiritual life, with the other an orthodox  creed: with the one the guiding principle is the individual conscience, with  the other an external rule of ordinances: with the one faith is allied to liberty, with the other to bondage. Thus it becomes a question, whether St James’s protest against reliance on faith alone has any reference, direct or indirect, to St Paul’s language and teaching; whether in fact it is not aimed against an entirely different type of religious feeling, against the Pharisaic spirit which rested satisfied with a barren orthodoxy fruitless in works of charity. Whether this is the true bearing of the Epistle of St James or not, must be determined by a close examination of its contents. 152  Ambiguity of the Hebrew.  Two ren- derings.  (i) Lxx and St Paul.  (ii) Judaic writers.  EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS,  The interpretation of Deut. xxi. 23.  This passage occupied an important place in the early controversies between the Christians and the Jews. Partly owing to this circumstance, and partly from the ambiguity of the Hebrew, it was variously interpreted and applied.  The words of the original are nbn ombds nbss 5, ‘for (the) curse of God (is) he that is hanged.’ The ambiguity arises out of the construction  of ombx, since the case attached to nddp may denote either the person  who pronounces the curse, as Judges ix. 57 (On)! nbbs) and 2 Sam. xvi. 12  anbdsp in the Q’ri), or the person against whom the curse is pronounced, as  Gen. xxvii. 13 (qnoSp) ; in other words, it represents either a subjective or an objective genitive. As we assign one or other sense therefore to the dependent case, we get two distinct interpretations.  1. ‘He that is hanged is accursed in the sight of God.” This is the rendering of the Lxx, xexatnpayévos vd Tov Ceod, adopted in substance, it would appear, by St Paul; and seems to have obtained the suffrages of most recent commentators whatever their opinions. It is certainly sup- ported by a more exact parallel (Judges ix. 57) than the alternative render- ing, and seems to suit the context better, for the sense will then be, ‘Do not let the body hang after sunset ; for the hanging body (of a malefactor) defiles the land, since the curse of God rests upon it,  2. The other rendering is, ‘He that hangeth is a contempt of, a reproach or insult to God.” ‘This seems to have been the popular Jewish interpretation (shared therefore by Jewish Christians) at all events from  the second century of the Christian era. The passage was so taken by  the Jewish or Ebionite translators, Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus}, It is explained in this way in the ancient Jewish commentary on Deutero- nomy, Siphri*, and in the so-called Targum of Jonathan*. This rendering appeared also in the Ebionite Gospel‘.
